source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ τὰς ἡρωϊκὰς ἱστορίας περὶ τῶν εἰς ᾅδου καταβεβηκέναι λεγομένων κἀκεῖθεν ἀνεληλυθέναι τερατείας εἶναί φησιν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος. ὡς τῶν ἡρώων ἀφανῶν γενομένων ἐπί τινα χρόνον καὶ ὑπεκκλεψάντων ἑαυτοὺς τῆς ὄψεως πάντων ἀνθρώπων καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιδειξάντων. ὡς ἀπὸ ᾅδου ἀνεληλυθότων (τοιαῦτα γὰρ ἔοικε περὶ τοῦ ἐν Ὀδρύσαις Ὀρφέως καὶ τοῦ ἐν Θεσσαλίᾳ Πρωτεσιλάου καὶ τοῦ ἐπὶ Ταινάρῳ Ἡρακλέος ἔτι δὲ καὶ περὶ Θησέως ἐμφαίνειν αὐτοῦ ἡ λέξις), φέρε παραστήσωμεν ὅτι οὐ δύναται τὸ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἱστορούμενον ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγηγέρθαι τούτοις παραβάλλεσθαι. ἕκαστος μὲν γὰρ τῶν λεγομένων κατὰ τοὺς τόπους ἡρώων βουληθεὶς ἂν ἐδυνήθη ἑαυτὸν ὑπεκκλέψαι τῆς ὄψεως τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ πάλιν κρίνας ἐπανελθεῖν πρὸς οὓς καταλέλοιπεν· Ἰησοῦ δὲ σταυρωθέντος ἐπὶ πάντων Ἰουδαίων καὶ καθαιρεθέντος αὐτοῦ τοῦ σώματος ἐν ὄψει τοῦ δήμου αὐτῶν, πῶς οἷόν τε τὸ παραπλήσιον πλάσασθαι λέγειν αὐτὸν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἱστορουμένοις ἥρωσιν εἰς ᾅδου καταβεβηκέναι κἀκεῖθεν ἀνεληλυθέναι; φαμὲν δ᾿ ὅτι μή ποτε πρὸς ἀπολογίαν τοῦ ἐσταυρῶσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν καὶ τοιοῦτον λέγοιτ᾿ ἂν, μάλιστα διὰ τὰ περὶ τῶν ἡρώων ἱστορηθέντα τῶν εἰς ᾅδου καταβεβηκέναι βίᾳ νομιζομένων, ὅτι εἰ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐτεθνήκει ἀσήμῳ θανάτῳ, οὐχ ὥστε δῆλος εἶναι ἀποθανὼν ὅλῳ τῷ δήμῳ τῶν Ἰουδαίων, εἶτα μετὰ τοῦτ᾿ ἀληθῶς ἦν ἀναστὰς ἐκ νεκρῶν, χώραν εἶχεν ἂν τὸ ὑπονοηθὲν περὶ τῶν ἡρώων καὶ περὶ τούτου λεχθῆναι. μή ποτ᾿ οὖν πρὸς ἄλλοις αἰτίοις τοῦ σταυρωθῆναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν καὶ τοῦτο δύναται συμβάλλεσθαι τῷ αὐτὸν ἐπισήμως ἐπὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ ἀποτεθνηκέναι, ἵνα μηδεὶς ἔχῃ λέγειν ὅτι ἑκὼν ὑπεξέστη τῆς ὄψεως τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἔδοξεν ἀποτεθνηκέναι οὐκ ἀποτέθνηκε δὲ (ἀλλ᾿) , ὅτ᾿ ἐβουλήθη, πάλιν ἐπιφανεὶς ἐτερατεύσατο τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν; σαφὲς δ᾿ οἶμαι καὶ ἐναργὲς εἶναι τὸ ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ ἐπιχείρημα, ἐπικινδύνῳ ὡς πρὸς τὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίον διδασκαλίᾳ ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιδεδωκότων, ἣν οὐκ ἂν πλασσόμενοι τὸ ἐγηγέρθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐκ νεκρῶν οὕτως εὐτόνως ἐδίδαξαν, μετὰ τοῦ καὶ αὐτοὶ οὐ μόνον ἑτέρους παρασκευάζειν πρὸς τὸ θανάτου καταφρονεῖν ἀλλ᾿ αὐτοὶ πολὺ πρότερον τοῦτο ποιεῖν.
pass_a_gloss: And since the Jew in Celsus says the heroic stories (ἡρωϊκαὶ ἱστορίαι) about those said to have gone down (καταβαίνω) into Hades and to have come up (ἀνέρχομαι) from there are marvel-mongerings (τερατεῖαι), as though the heroes (ἥρωες) became invisible (ἀφανεῖς) for some time and stole themselves away (ὑπεκκλέπτω) from the sight (ὄψις) of all men and after these showed (ἐπιδείκνυμι) themselves as having come up from Hades (for his wording (λέξις) seems to indicate (ἐμφαίνω) such things about Orpheus among the Odrysians and Protesilaus in Thessaly and Heracles at Taenarum and further also about Theseus), come, let us establish (παρίστημι) that what is narrated (ἱστορέω) about Jesus, to have been raised (ἐγείρω, pf.) from the dead (νεκροί), cannot be compared (παραβάλλω) to these. For each of the heroes spoken of according to the places (τόποι), having wished, could have stolen himself away from the sight of men and again, having decided (κρίνω), returned (ἐπανέρχομαι) to those he had left (καταλείπω); but Jesus having been crucified (σταυρόω) before all Jews and his body (σῶμα) having been taken down (καθαιρέω) in sight of their people (δῆμος), how is it possible to fabricate (πλάσσω) the like, to say he, like the narrated heroes, went down into Hades and came up from there? And we say that perhaps (μή ποτε) toward a defence (ἀπολογία) of Jesus' having been crucified such a thing too might be said, especially because of the things narrated about the heroes thought (νομίζω) to have gone down into Hades by force (βίᾳ): that if by supposition (καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν) Jesus had died an unmarked/obscure (ἄσημος) death, not so as to be evident (δῆλος) as having died to the whole people of the Jews, then after this had truly risen from the dead, there would have been room (χώρα) for what was suspected (ὑπονοέω) about the heroes to be said also about this one. Perhaps then, besides other causes (αἴτια) of Jesus' being crucified, this too can contribute (συμβάλλομαι) to his having died conspicuously (ἐπισήμως) on the cross (σταυρός): so that no one may have [ground] to say that he willingly (ἑκών) withdrew (ὑπεξίσταμαι) from the sight of men and seemed (δοκέω) to have died but had not died, but, when he wished, appearing (ἐπιφαίνομαι) again made a marvel (τερατεύομαι) of the resurrection (ἀνάστασις) from the dead. And clear (σαφής) and evident (ἐναργής), I think, is the argument (ἐπιχείρημα) from his disciples (μαθηταί), who gave themselves over (ἐπιδίδωμι) to a teaching (διδασκαλία) dangerous (ἐπικίνδυνος) as regards the life (βίος) of men, which, if fabricating Jesus' having been raised from the dead, they would not have taught so vigorously (εὐτόνως), with the fact that they themselves not only prepared (παρασκευάζω) others toward despising (καταφρονέω) death but themselves did this much earlier.
pass_b_english: The Jew in Celsus says that the heroic tales of those who are said to have gone down to Hades and come back up from there are marvel-mongering, taking it that the heroes vanished for a time, stole themselves away from the sight of all men, and afterwards showed themselves as though they had come back up from Hades. For his words seem to suggest something of this kind about Orpheus among the Odrysians, Protesilaus in Thessaly, Heracles at Taenarum, and Theseus too. Come, then, let us show that the account of Jesus’ being raised from the dead cannot be compared with these.

For each of the heroes spoken of in those places could, had he wished, have stolen himself away from human sight and, when he decided, gone back again to those he had left. But since Jesus was crucified before all the Jews, and his body was taken down in the sight of their people (compare John 19:38), how is it possible to invent a like tale, saying that he, like the heroes of the stories, went down to Hades and came back up from there?

We say, too, that perhaps something like this might also be said in defence of Jesus’ crucifixion, especially because of the stories told about the heroes who are thought to have gone down to Hades by force: that if, for the sake of argument, Jesus had died an obscure death, so that his death was not evident to the whole people of the Jews, and then after that had truly risen from the dead, there would have been room for what was suspected about the heroes to be said about him too. Perhaps, then, besides other reasons why Jesus was crucified, this too may contribute to his having died openly on the cross, so that no one could say that he withdrew from human sight of his own accord, and seemed to have died but had not died, but, when he wished, appeared again and staged a marvel of rising from the dead.

Clear and evident, I think, is the argument drawn from his disciples. They gave themselves to a teaching that put their lives in danger, and they would not have taught it with such vigour if they had made up the claim that Jesus had been raised from the dead; and all the while they not only prepared others to despise death but themselves did so long before.

choices.why: John 19:38 marked 'compare' (allusion to the taking down, not a quotation)
ἵνα μηδεὶς ἔχῃ λέγειν: colon -> 'so that no one could say', making the purpose explicit
μετὰ τοῦ ... ποιεῖν joined to the preceding clause ('and all the while...') instead of a loose 'Besides'
βίᾳ νομιζομένων read as 'by force' kept; ambiguity already flagged in translator_notes

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

2.56: βίᾳ νομιζομένων is kept as 'thought to have gone down to Hades by force'. The phrase could also mean 'hardly believed' or 'believed against the evidence'. The translator's notes already flag this; the owner may want to rule on it, but the current reading can be defended, so the section passed.

translator_notes: βίᾳ νομιζομένων (‘thought to have gone down to Hades by force’) is taken with the heroes (Heracles and Theseus forced their way into Hades); the phrase is compressed and could also mean ‘thought, against the evidence, to have gone down’. The source shows a doubled αὐτὸν αὐτὸν in ‘λέγειν αὐτὸν αὐτὸν’; read as one αὐτόν (‘saying that he’). (ἀλλ᾿) is an editor’s supplement, translated (‘but’). μή ποτε twice rendered ‘perhaps’, as Origen offers a tentative reason. Taking down of the body in public: John 19:38 (compare Luke 23:53); allusion, not quotation. Jesus’ descent to Hades is raised here only as the opponent’s comparison and is not cited. The disciples’ readiness to die is not tied to one verse and is left uncited.
